title: The Deer-eyed Girl's Multiplication
devanagari: छिन्नास्तेन गुणेन ते च गुणिता जाताः कति स्युर्वद॥
iast: pañca-try-eka-mitā divākara-guṇā aṅkāḥ kati syur yadi |
chinnās tena guṇena te ca guṇitā jātāḥ kati syur vada ||
translation: O girl, Lilavati, with eyes as restless as a young deer's! If you are clever, O fair one, at multiplying whole, by places, by factors and by parts, tell me: the number written five-three-one, multiplied by the suns, what does it become? And when that product is divided by the same multiplier, what comes back?
translation_hi: हे बाला लीलावती, हिरन के बच्चे जैसी चंचल आँखों वाली! हे कल्याणी, यदि तुम पूर्ण संख्या, स्थान, विभाग और खंड विधि से गुणा करने में कुशल हो, तो बताओ कि पाँच-तीन-एक वाली संख्या को 'सूर्यों' से गुणा करने पर क्या मिलता है? और उस गुणनफल को उसी गुणक से भाग देने पर क्या बचता है?

words.note: Digits are read right to left: 5, 3, 1 → 135.
divākara (sun) = 12 in word numerals, for the 12 Ādityas.
Multiplying by the whole multiplier at once.
Multiplying digit by digit, place by place.
Splitting the multiplier into a sum: 12 = 8 + 4.
Literally 'cut'. √chid, as in -cchid in the Tāṇḍava stotra!

grammar: Word numerals: दिवाकर (sun) = 12, for the twelve Ādityas. पञ्च-त्रि-एक read right to left = 135. See the Grammar page for the full table.
Division is 'cutting': छिन्न 'cut' from √छिद्. The same root gives -च्छिद् 'destroyer' in Tāṇḍava verse 9.
Optative: स्युः 'would be', the mood for 'if…, what would…'.
Yaṇ sandhi: त्रि + एक → त्र्येक. इ before a different vowel becomes य्.
question: What is 135 × 12?
solution:
Whole (rūpa): 135 × 12 = 1620

By places (sthāna): 135 × 1 = 135 and 135 × 2 = 270, placed one step apart: 1350 + 270 = 1620

By factors (vibhāga): 12 = 3 × 4, so 135 × 3 = 405, then 405 × 4 = 1620

By parts (khaṇḍa): 12 = 8 + 4, so 135 × 8 + 135 × 4 = 1080 + 540 = 1620

Divided back by 12: 1620 ÷ 12 = 135

Science link: the 'factors' and 'parts' methods are the distributive and associative laws. Computers still multiply by splitting numbers into parts: Karatsuba's fast multiplication algorithm (1960) is a clever khaṇḍa method.
